valuation_approach: Kiwi Property is a New Zealand internally-managed REIT. Statutory NetIncome is dominated by non-cash fair-value movements on investment properties and interest-rate derivatives (FY26 NPAT was $50.4m, down 11.5% YoY despite an 8.6% rise in operating profit before tax, because valuation/derivative marks swung the other way; H1-2026 NPAT fell 77.3% on a $30.3m unrealised fair-value loss) -- it is NOT a proxy for earnings power and should not drive a WACC-based free-cash-flow DCF. The correct valuation frame is (1) capitalisation of Adjusted Funds From Operations (AFFO) / distributable income at a cost of equity, since AFFO is already stated after interest expense -- net debt must NEVER be subtracted from an AFFO-capitalised value -- and (2) cross-checking against reported Net Tangible Assets (NTA) per share and the portfolio's traded discount/premium to NTA. Key latest data points: NTA per share $1.12 (30-Sep-2025 and again 31-Mar-2026, each down ~2.2-2.4% over the respective period); FY26 AFFO $100.2m (+8.0% YoY) with a payout ratio of ~92% of AFFO; FY27 dividend guidance 5.75 cps (+2.7% on FY26's 5.60 cps), with the first FY27 quarterly instalment of 1.4375 cps paid 18-Sep-2026; pro forma gearing 33.3% post the ASB North Wharf settlement (31-Mar-2026), down from 38.5% at 30-Sep-2025 and 38.4% at FY25; total portfolio value approximately $3.0 billion (31-Mar-2026, down 0.9% for the year); shares on issue ~1,625m and growing via an active DRP. S&P Global rates Kiwi Property's issuer credit BBB/Stable (green bonds BBB+, one notch higher, secured). Consensus analyst price target sits at roughly $1.07-1.12 (Buy-leaning, ~2 buy/2 hold, 0 sell across 4 analysts) versus a share price recently around $0.88-0.95, implying mid-teens percentage upside to NTA/consensus fair value.
overview: Kiwi Property Group is New Zealand's largest listed diversified real estate investment trust, internally managed and NZX Main Board-listed (fixed-rate green bonds also trade on the NZX Debt Market). The company owns and develops a portfolio of large-format 'retail-led mixed-use' town centres (Sylvia Park, LynnMall, The Base), premium Auckland/Wellington office towers, and a nascent build-to-rent (BTR) residential business (Resido, at Sylvia Park), alongside an early-stage large-format-retail/residential greenfield development at Drury, south Auckland. Total portfolio value was approximately $3.0-3.3 billion as at FY26/H1-2026, concentrated 84%+ in Auckland.

business_model.summary: Kiwi Property earns recurring net rental income from long-leased retail, office and (increasingly) build-to-rent residential assets, supplemented by land-sale proceeds from its Drury development pipeline and, from FY2025-26, a funds-management stake (Mackersy Property) that provides fee income and an alternative capital source. Distributions to shareholders are set at 90-100% of Adjusted Funds From Operations (AFFO), a REIT-standard non-GAAP cash-earnings measure.

revenue_streams.name: Mixed-use (Sylvia Park, LynnMall, The Base, Drury)
Office (Vero Centre, ASB North Wharf sold, The Aurora Centre)
Retail (The Plaza sold FY26, Centre Place North)
Other (incl. held-for-sale assets, BTR/Resido, funds-management/property fees)

business_model.customer_type: B2B (national and international retail/office tenants -- anchor tenants include Woolworths/Foodstuffs-affiliated supermarkets, ASB Bank, major fashion and F&B chains, IKEA as an adjacent anchor) plus a new B2C build-to-rent residential tenant base at Resido (295 apartments, 99% leased as at Sep-2025)
business_model.geographic_mix: Auckland ~84% of portfolio value ('golden triangle' core), Hamilton ~8%, Wellington ~4%, Palmerston North exposure removed (The Plaza sold during FY26); 100% New Zealand, no offshore assets
business_model.revenue_recurrence: Predominantly long-dated contracted rental income (multi-year retail/office leases with fixed reviews) plus BTR residential leases (12 months to 10 years); Drury land sales are transactional/one-off and timed to FY27-FY29

main_competitors: Goodman Property Trust (GMT.NZ) -- NZ's largest listed industrial/logistics landlord
Stride Property Group (SPG.NZ) -- retail/office including NorthWest Shopping Centre
Vital Healthcare Property Trust -- healthcare REIT
Scentre Group / Vicinity Centres (ASX) -- larger-scale Australian mall operators, indirect competitive benchmark for retail-led mixed-use format
Foodstuffs/Woolworths NZ-anchored competing malls and big-box centres
competitive_position.market_position: Largest diversified listed property company on the NZX by portfolio value and a constituent of the S&P/NZX 20; owns New Zealand's largest shopping centre (Sylvia Park, ~16m+ visits/yr) which anchors the group's 'retail-led mixed-use' positioning; a distant second-tier player versus Goodman (industrial, larger index weight) and Precinct (premium CBD office) in their respective sub-sectors

moat_factors.description: Sylvia Park, LynnMall and The Base sit on large, strategically located land banks near transport nodes in Auckland's high-growth corridor; the cost and regulatory difficulty of assembling comparable sites is a structural barrier to new large-format competition

Long-standing relationships with supermarket, banking (ASB 9-year lease extension to 2040) and international retail anchors (IKEA opened adjacent to Sylvia Park Dec-2025, with an airbridge connecting the two) reinforce footfall and negotiating leverage
In-house capability to densify existing land banks into retail+office+BTR 'halo effect' communities is a differentiated, hard-to-replicate skill versus single-format landlords
BBB/Stable issuer rating (BBB+ on secured green bonds) and access to bank, bond and now funds-management (Mackersy) capital sources

weaknesses: Small scale versus Australian mall operators (Scentre, Vicinity) and versus Goodman's industrial platform -- limited ability to compete for very large capital allocations
Auckland concentration (~84% of portfolio) leaves the company exposed to a single metro market's economic cycle, population growth assumptions and any localised oversupply
Historically high gearing (38%+ through FY25/H1-26, only reduced to low-30s% post asset sales) constrains balance-sheet flexibility relative to some peers
Office segment (~24% of portfolio) faces structural post-COVID demand headwinds despite recent ASB and Vero Centre leasing wins
BTR/Resido is a first-of-its-kind, unproven format in New Zealand -- yield-on-cost and long-term regulatory treatment (tenancy law, rent stabilisation risk) remain relatively untested locally
Drury stage-one internal rate of return came in at 18% versus management's own 20% target, a modest miss on one of five FY26 executive scorecard goals

growth_drivers: Sylvia Park expansion and densification (southern enhancement, Pedestrian Plaza, Asian supermarket, additional mixed-use floors) leveraging the halo effect from IKEA's December 2025 opening and connecting airbridge, which lifted Sylvia Park precinct foot traffic ~8% in the following four months
Resido/BTR scaling: initial 295-apartment lease-up completed (99% leased Sep-2025, rents ~26% above Auckland median), validating the model for potential further BTR development at other KPG sites

Drury greenfield development (Auckland's next major metropolitan centre candidate): ~77% of the large-format-retail precinct conditionally sold (Costco, Rebel Sport/Briscoes, Harvey Norman, Foodstuffs) with proceeds to date of ~$115m and further staged proceeds expected FY27-FY29

Asset recycling out of lower-conviction office/retail into the core mixed-use strategy: The Plaza sold ($118.9m, FY26) and ASB North Wharf sold to Precinct Pacific Investment LP (~$205-210m, settled 29-May-2026), together delivering $320m+ of redeployable capital and cutting pro forma gearing to 33.3%

Mackersy Property partnership: convertible loan converted to a 50% equity stake (Dec-2025) in a $2bn+ AUM funds manager, providing a new off-balance-sheet capital source (the new Mackersy Large Format Retail Fund, seeded with Sylvia Park Lifestyle) to fund further LFR development without diluting KPG's own balance sheet

Falling New Zealand interest rates (RBNZ cutting cycle) reducing funding costs -- weighted average interest rate already down from 5.30% (Mar-2025) to 4.89% (Sep-2025) -- and providing scope for cap-rate stabilisation/compression on the investment portfolio

Proposed earthquake-prone building (EPB) regulatory reform (announced Sep-2025, legislation expected 2026) would remove Auckland from the EPB regime entirely, reducing expected seismic remediation cost provisions embedded in valuations
Specialty retail sales recovery: mixed-use portfolio sales and foot traffic broadly stable to slightly positive through FY26 as consumer spending stabilises alongside the RBNZ easing cycle

business.description: ~84% of portfolio value is in Auckland; a localised downturn, oversupply of retail/BTR stock, or population growth disappointment disproportionately affects the whole portfolio
Long-run online retail penetration is a structural headwind to physical mall footfall and specialty tenant sales, partially offset by the 'destination' and mixed-use strategy
Hybrid working has structurally reduced office space demand; Vero Centre occupancy improved to 94.3% (Sep-2025) but ~2 floors remain vacant, and the segment is being actively shrunk via divestment

Resido is New Zealand's first large-scale BTR project; long-run occupancy, rental growth, maintenance capex and yield-on-cost are unproven at scale locally, and the Auckland rental market saw supply outpacing demand during initial lease-up
Drury stage-one IRR came in at 18% against an internal 20% target, illustrating that even 'successful' development monetisation can undershoot underwriting assumptions

financial.description: ~$1.29bn of interest-bearing liabilities (bank debt + green bonds) at a weighted average rate of 4.89% (Sep-2025); KPG040 $100m green bond matured Nov-2025 and was refinanced via increased bank facilities; ongoing rollover of remaining green bonds (KPG050/060/070 tranches) and bank facilities exposes the company to future rate and spread risk

Gearing was 38.5% at H1-2026 (up from 38.4% FY25), above management's comfort level, though the ASB North Wharf settlement reduced pro forma gearing to 33.3% by FY26 year-end; covenant compliance has been maintained but leaves less capacity for opportunistic investment

Active DRP (retaining tens of millions of dollars of equity per half) is funding capex but steadily increases share count (~1,594.6m weighted-average FY25 to ~1,625m+ shares), diluting per-share metrics over time

regulatory.description: Proposed reform (announced Sep-2025) is expected to be a net positive for KPG (removing Auckland from the EPB regime) but legislative timing/detail is not yet finalised (expected enactment 2026)

regulatory.risk: Residential tenancy law changes affecting BTR
regulatory.description: As a large-scale BTR landlord, KPG is exposed to future changes in residential tenancy legislation (rent controls, notice periods) that could affect Resido economics

macro.description: New Zealand economy exited recession only slowly; mixed-use tenant sales growth has been modest through FY26, with recovery contingent on continued rate cuts flowing through to household spending

Property valuations are directly sensitive to capitalisation and discount rate assumptions; portfolio value fell 0.9% in FY26 and NTA per share declined 2.2-2.4% across successive periods on cap-rate/discount-rate driven fair-value losses, and further rate volatility could reverse recent stabilisation
Ongoing Drury and Sylvia Park development exposes KPG to construction cost escalation, though staged/matched-to-sales capital deployment mitigates this

execution.description: Multiple board changes over FY25-26 (Jane Freeman and Mary Jane Daly departed, Kevin Kenrick and Michele Embling joined); Chair Simon Shakesheff and CEO Clive Mackenzie provide continuity. CEO achieved 4 of 5 FY26 performance goals (Drury IRR the one miss), total pay $1.78m (+14% YoY)

Large-format retail land sale proceeds at Drury are conditional and staggered across FY27-FY29; delays (as already experienced versus original timelines) would push back balance-sheet deleveraging and reinvestment capacity

The Nov-2024 investment and subsequent Dec-2025 conversion to a 50% equity stake in a funds-management business is a new line of business/earnings source for KPG, requiring successful governance and fund-raising execution (e.g. the LFR Fund's capital raise / Sylvia Park Lifestyle sale)

macro_factors.industry_outlook: NZ listed real estate (S&P/NZX Real Estate Select Index) has been broadly flat to negative over recent years amid a higher-rate, recession-affected environment, but has shown signs of stabilisation/recovery through FY26 as the RBNZ cutting cycle progresses and cap rates stabilise
macro_factors.cyclicality: Moderate-to-high -- retail tenant sales and office demand are sensitive to the NZ economic cycle; property valuations are directly geared to interest rate and cap-rate movements, amplifying NTA volatility relative to underlying rental cash flows
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: High -- both (1) funding cost on ~$1.29bn of debt (weighted average rate already down from 5.30% to 4.89% over H1-2026 as rates fall) and (2) capitalisation/discount rates used in investment property valuations, which directly move NTA and reported (non-cash) profit/loss
macro_factors.currency_exposure: None -- 100% New Zealand dollar revenue, assets and debt; no direct FX exposure
key_input_costs: Construction/development costs (Drury, Sylvia Park enhancement, Vero Centre upgrade)
Interest expense on bank debt and green bonds
Seismic remediation/strengthening costs embedded in valuations
macro_factors.regulatory_trend: Net positive -- proposed earthquake-prone building law reform expected to reduce remediation cost provisions for Auckland-concentrated portfolios like KPG's

recent_developments.event: FY27 Q1 dividend of 1.4375 cps paid (imputation credits 0.428642 cps, supplementary dividend 0.194510 cps for non-resident shareholders); record date 3-Sep-2026, in line with the FY27 full-year guidance of 5.75 cps

FY26 annual results (year ended 31-Mar-2026): net rental income $202.4m (+4.3%), operating profit before tax $126.2m (+8.6%), AFFO $100.2m (+8.0%), net profit after tax $50.4m (-11.5% YoY on adverse fair-value/derivative swings), portfolio value ~$3.0bn (-0.9% for the year), NTA per share $1.12 (-2.4%); dividend of 5.60 cps confirmed (+3.7% YoY)

CEO Clive Mackenzie's FY26 scorecard: 4 of 5 performance goals met (AFFO growth, non-core asset recycling, Drury stage-one land sales, Sylvia Park/IKEA enhancement), with the Drury stage-one IRR target missed (18% actual vs 20% goal); total CEO pay $1.78m, up 14% YoY

~$205-210m sale of ASB North Wharf office building (Wynyard Quarter) to Precinct Pacific Investment Limited Partnership settled after clearing Overseas Investment Office approval, reducing pro forma gearing to 33.3%
IKEA opened adjacent to Sylvia Park with a connecting airbridge; Sylvia Park precinct foot traffic rose ~8% in the following four months, validating the mixed-use 'halo effect' thesis

Mackersy Property convertible loan converted to equity, giving Kiwi Property a 50% shareholding in the ~$2bn AUM funds-management business; new Mackersy Large Format Retail Fund established, seeded with Sylvia Park Lifestyle, expected to release at least $53m of capital (subsequently agreed at ~$90m sale price)
$100m KPG040 green bond matured and was repaid, refinanced via a $135m increase in bank debt facilities
ASB signed a 9-year lease extension at ASB North Wharf through to 2040, ahead of the building's subsequent sale

Net rental income growth 7.0%; operating profit before tax $62.9m (+11.5%); net profit after tax $9.8m (-77.3%) on a $30.3m unrealised fair-value loss; AFFO +7.2%; NTA per share $1.12 (-2.2%); gearing 38.5%; Resido lease-up completed at 99%; The Plaza and Sylvia Park Lifestyle reclassified to held-for-sale
NZ Government announced proposed earthquake-prone building regulatory reform that would remove Auckland from the EPB regime, a potential positive for KPG's seismic cost provisions

First unconditional Drury large-format-retail land sale to Foodstuffs (April 2025), followed by conditional sales to Costco Wholesale (6.4ha), Rebel Sport/Briscoes and Harvey Norman (October 2025), taking total conditionally-sold Drury LFR land to ~77% of the precinct, with proceeds to date of ~$115m
The Plaza (Palmerston North) sold for $118.9m, exiting KPG's regional retail exposure as part of the shift toward a smaller number of large, Auckland-centric mixed-use assets

guidance.as_of: FY26 Annual Results, 18-May-2026, confirmed via the FY27 Q1 dividend payment 18-Sep-2026

items.notes: +2.7% on the FY26 dividend of 5.60 cps (which was itself +3.7% on FY25); expected within the 90-100% AFFO payout policy, at the higher end of the range; first Q1 instalment of 1.4375 cps paid 18-Sep-2026, consistent with the guided full-year rate; contingent on financial performance and absent material adverse events
Standing dividend policy; FY26 actual payout was ~92% of AFFO

items.target: Reduce below FY25/H1-26 levels (38.4-38.5%) via asset recycling
items.notes: Pro forma gearing reached 33.3% at 31-Mar-2026 following the ASB North Wharf settlement, a material improvement versus the 38%+ levels through FY25 and H1-2026

items.target: Staged proceeds, ~77% of LFR precinct conditionally sold, ~$115m proceeds to date
items.notes: Capital spend at Drury is matched to land sales achieved; no lump-sum guidance given, timing pushed out versus original expectations due to slower transaction markets; stage-one IRR of 18% came in below the internal 20% target

items.target: Held below prior-year levels as % of net property income
items.notes: Cost discipline target beaten in FY25 (12.7% vs 14.3% ceiling); H1-2026 expenses down 5% YoY on a normalised basis; management continues to emphasise cost control into FY27

guidance.management_commentary: Management (Chair Simon Shakesheff and CEO Clive Mackenzie) frame FY26/27 around four repeated strategic priorities: (1) balance sheet management and asset recycling (Plaza and ASB North Wharf sales, Mackersy partnership as an alternative capital source), (2) driving rent growth (total rental growth +3.5% in H1-2026, IKEA halo effect lifting Sylvia Park foot traffic), (3) staged Drury monetisation, and (4) cost discipline. CEO Mackenzie's FY26 scorecard shows 4 of 5 goals met, with Drury stage-one returns undershooting target. Management describes the business as 'well positioned to benefit from improving economic conditions' as NZ interest rates fall, while flagging 'ongoing macroeconomic and geopolitical volatility' as a caveat on all forward guidance.

reit_metrics.nta_per_share: $1.12 (as at 30-Sep-2025 and again 31-Mar-2026, each down ~2.2-2.4% over the respective period on cap-rate-driven fair-value losses)
reit_metrics.gearing_lvr: 38.5% (30-Sep-2025, H1-2026) improving to a pro forma 33.3% (31-Mar-2026) after the ASB North Wharf sale settlement
reit_metrics.dividend_per_share: FY25 actual 5.475 cps cash (6.664 cps gross incl. imputation); FY26 actual 5.60 cps (+3.7%); FY27 guided 5.75 cps (+2.7%), Q1 FY27 instalment of 1.4375 cps paid 18-Sep-2026; paid quarterly
reit_metrics.portfolio_value: Approximately $3.0-3.3bn (FY25/H1-2026), reducing to ~$3.0bn by FY26 year-end reflecting both a ~0.9% fair-value decline and the sale of ASB North Wharf/The Plaza out of the portfolio
reit_metrics.affo: FY25 $92.8m (-7.0% YoY, impacted by the removal of building tax depreciation and higher interest costs); H1-2026 +7.2% YoY; FY26 full year $100.2m (+8.0%)
reit_metrics.credit_rating: S&P Global BBB/Stable issuer rating; green bonds rated BBB+ (one notch higher, secured)
reit_metrics.current_price_vs_nta: Share price ~$0.88-0.95 (Sep-2026, 52-week range $0.88-$1.145) versus NTA $1.12 implies a P/NTA of roughly 0.78-0.85x, i.e. trading at a 15-22% discount to book; analyst consensus price target ~$1.07-1.12 (Buy-leaning, 2 buy/2 hold/0 sell across 4 analysts) implies mid-teens percentage upside; dividend yield ~6.9% vs an NZ listed-property sector average closer to 5.6%

bull_case: Irreplaceable Sylvia Park land bank plus the newly validated 'halo effect' (IKEA opening and connecting airbridge lifted precinct foot traffic ~8%) supports above-market rental growth in the core mixed-use segment (total leasing spreads +3.2-3.5% in H1-2026 despite a weak consumer backdrop)

Balance sheet transformation well underway: pro forma gearing fell from 38.5% to 33.3% within months (ASB North Wharf + The Plaza sales), materially de-risking the covenant position and funding further reinvestment without dilutive equity raises

Resido BTR proof-of-concept succeeded -- fully leased in under 12 months at rents ~26% above the Auckland median -- opening a credible new growth vertical (further BTR at other KPG sites) and validating the wider mixed-use residential thesis

Falling NZ interest rates are a direct tailwind on two fronts: lower funding costs (weighted average rate already down 41bp to 4.89% in six months) and potential cap-rate compression reversing recent NTA declines

Trading at a meaningful discount to NTA (~0.78-0.85x) with a ~6.9% cash dividend yield and FY27 dividend guidance raised again (+2.7%, first quarterly instalment already paid), offering income plus a re-rating catalyst if the discount narrows as gearing falls and Drury proceeds materialise; analyst consensus price target (~$1.07-1.12) implies mid-teens upside
bear_case: Reported NTA has declined for multiple consecutive periods (-2.2% to -2.4% in successive halves) on cap-rate/discount-rate driven fair-value losses, and FY26 statutory net profit fell 11.5% YoY despite operating profit growth -- a reminder that further rate volatility or a stalled NZ recovery could keep eroding book value even as operating metrics improve

Heavy single-metro concentration (~84% Auckland) leaves KPG fully exposed to one city's population growth, office-demand and retail-spending assumptions, with no geographic diversification to cushion a local downturn

Office segment still carries structural post-COVID demand risk despite recent leasing wins (Vero Centre 94.3% occupied, ASB extension to 2040); remaining vacancy and any future tenant losses would pressure both income and valuation

Drury monetisation -- a key deleveraging and growth lever -- has already slipped versus original timelines, delivered a stage-one IRR of 18% versus an internal 20% target, and remains conditional/staged across FY27-FY29, so realised proceeds and returns could disappoint again

BTR/Resido is an unproven format at scale in New Zealand; the initial lease-up succeeded, but long-run rental growth, maintenance capex intensity, and any future residential tenancy law changes are largely untested for a listed NZ landlord
Active Dividend Reinvestment Plan steadily grows the share count, diluting per-share NTA and distributable income growth even as headline dividend-per-share guidance rises modestly
